report:
## Conclusion

The claim is **false for the general population**. Multiple controlled studies measuring actual blood gases and CO2 concentrations found that healthy people, and even patients with moderate-to-severe COPD, show no clinically significant change in oxygen or CO2 levels while wearing surgical or cloth masks for extended periods. A study on "Effect of Face Masks on Gas Exchange in Healthy Persons and Patients with COPD" found no meaningful oxygen restriction or CO2 buildup (foxnews.com). Direct measurement of CO2 concentration inside masks found levels around 2,000–3,000 ppm during activity—elevated versus ambient air (500–900 ppm) but far below the ~40,000+ ppm threshold associated with acute physiological harm, and not indicative of dangerous hypercapnia (https://aaqr.org/articles/aaqr-20-07-covid-0403.pdf). USA Today's fact-check similarly concludes wearing a mask does not cause hypoxia or hypercapnia in healthy individuals, noting mask materials are porous enough for CO2 molecules (much smaller than viral particles) to escape (https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/factcheck/2020/05/30/fact-check-wearing-face-mask-not-cause-hypoxia-hypercapnia/5260106002/). Science Feedback's expert review reached the same conclusion (https://science.feedback.org/review/the-use-of-face-masks-reduces-the-transmission-of-covid-19-and-doesnt-lead-to-oxygen-deficiency-or-carbon-dioxide-buildup-in-the-bloodstream/).

**Caveat:** Research on people with chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure requiring non-invasive ventilation shows mask tolerance and gas exchange effects can differ and remain understudied in this specific vulnerable population—but this is not evidence of danger for the general public wearing masks for typical daily use.

**Overall:** For healthy individuals and even most patients with lung disease, prolonged mask use does not cause dangerous CO2 buildup.
